article_text:
Art Week Paris

Portrait of a Paris Art Week on Fire

On protest, business as usual, and the surreal experience of attending an art fair while smelling burning plastic.

Hyperallergic )

PARIS — “The people in the art world are courageous,” a collector told me at Asia Now, the first of the Paris art fairs that opened early in the week on Monday, in the heat of the protests. “But I would still like to be back at my hotel before 7pm, you know, just in case.”

Anyone who is a regular at Paris Art Week has a collection of stories about something going wrong. In 2022, there were strikes and cost-of-living marches. In October 2023, France was on high terror alert, and one of the bomb threats that emptied the airports of the country’s major cities led to, among other things, my plane landing in the middle of the French countryside. A couple of trains later, and voilà : I was in Paris in time for the vernissages.

This time, when I rolled my suitcase out of the Gare du Nord station late on the afternoon of Saturday, October 17, I was prepared. I breathed in the crisp air and smelled the burning plastic and walked past the black-clad protesters running from squads of police while firefighters put out scattered fires. I was supposed to meet a friend who lives in the Marais later that evening, but she couldn’t get home. She had planned a quiet, aesthetic weekend with her family to see shows and the art fair; she had even planned her outfits. What she found instead on Boulevard de Sébastopol, at the edge of her neighborhood, was the police playing cat and mouse with protesters.

“We had to run!” she told me. “When the police start hitting, they hit indiscriminately.” She had just come back from the Portuguese city of Porto, where local officers charged a peaceful housing-rights camp at 3 am , while people were still half asleep in their tents.

Around 11pm, she and her family finally made it home, closed the door behind them, and breathed a sigh of relief.

Ready for Art Week?

The Eve of Destruction

“I think the art fairs, in this context, are rather grotesque,” French-Moroccan artist El Mehdi Largo, who is skipping them all this year, tells me. “Then again, art fairs are pretty grotesque in any context.”

We are sitting in a café on rue Poissonnière, with a view of smashed glass and clusters of burned bikes that looked like the melted surfaces of Alberto Burri’s Combustioni .

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Audiences can’t get enough of Elizabeth Holmes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eight years after Theranos, her blood-testing startup collapsed in spectacular fashion, “ You Can See Everything ,” a gonzo documentary about Holmes, opened to a staggering $15 million from 855 screens. That ranks as the second-best opening for a non-music documentary in history, just behind 2004’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which debuted to $23.9 million. Remember, however, that Michael Moore’s takedown of Bushism was released in the hothouse atmosphere of an election year. “You Can See Everything” comes after Holmes has been everywhere for nearly a decade, popping up in podcasts, in documentaries from the likes of Alex Gibney, in best-sellers, and on TV, where she was memorably portrayed by Amanda Seyfried.", "links": [{"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/you-can-see-everything/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/YCSE_NP_1.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'You Can See Everything'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_A1332_e4d22d.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Melissa Yerou, Jamie King, Tracy Rosenblum and Christian Zilko at IndieWire Future of Filmmaking Summit held at Lumen on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet A24 was able to maintain interest in the convicted fraudster, teasing out the secrets that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ‘s documentary promised to disclose without ever revealing its surprises. Audiences intent on not having the whole thing spoiled snapped up tickets, with A24 reporting that there were more than 2,000 sellouts.", "links": [{"text": "A24", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/a24/"}, {"text": "Nathan Fielder", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/nathan-fielder/"}, {"text": "Lance Oppenheim", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/lance-oppenheim/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film ‘s success is a testament to a clever marketing campaign that by revealing next to nothing, somehow made “You Can See Everything” even more of an event . It’s also a credit to Nathan Fielder, the film’s co-director, who has cultivated a strong following through shows like Comedy Central’s “Nathan for You” and HBO’s “The Rehearsal,” that push meta to the breaking point. His awkward energy seemed perfectly matched for whatever Holmes is serving up through those unblinking eyes. Fielder’s co-director, Lance Oppenheim, is also riding high, having recently directed another A24 hit , the Robert Pattinson drama “Primetime.” That look at “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen has grossed nearly $45 million on a $14.5 million budget. “You Can See Everything” carries a $7 million budget, setting itself up for a very, very profitable run.", "links": [{"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "even more of an event", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/you-can-see-everything-a24-hopes-preserve-secrets-elizabeth-holmes-1235222048/"}, {"text": "another A24 hit", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/box-office/a24-primetime-box-office-opening-robert-pattinson-star-power-1235218868/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Last year at this time, A24 was in rough shape . It had raised $75 million in 2024 from Thrive Capital which valued the company at a massive $3.5 billion. Then it used that money to invest in some real duds, including “The Smashing Machine,” which cost $50 million and was supposed to score Dwayne Johnson an Oscar until it sunk like a rock at the box office , grossing a measly $21.1 million. Other costly flops included Ari Aster “Eddington,” which offered a return to the COVID era that audiences roundly rejected.", "links": [{"text": "in rough shape", "url": "https://variety.com/2025/film/box-office/one-battle-after-another-lose-100-million-dollars-theaters-1236552914/"}, {"text": "score Dwayne Johnson an Oscar", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/06/dwayne-johnson-smashing-machine-oscars-snub-lit-fire-1236954373/"}, {"text": "box office", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/box-office/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But since “Marty Supreme” opened in December of 2025, A24 has been on an epic hot streak. The drama about a ping-pong player became A24’s highest-grossing release ever, earning $192.4 million on a $70 million budget. But that record didn’t last long. “Backrooms” premiered in the summer, grossing more than $400 million on a $10 million budget. article_text:
Audiences can’t get enough of Elizabeth Holmes.

Eight years after Theranos, her blood-testing startup collapsed in spectacular fashion, “ You Can See Everything ,” a gonzo documentary about Holmes, opened to a staggering $15 million from 855 screens. That ranks as the second-best opening for a non-music documentary in history, just behind 2004’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which debuted to $23.9 million. Remember, however, that Michael Moore’s takedown of Bushism was released in the hothouse atmosphere of an election year. “You Can See Everything” comes after Holmes has been everywhere for nearly a decade, popping up in podcasts, in documentaries from the likes of Alex Gibney, in best-sellers, and on TV, where she was memorably portrayed by Amanda Seyfried.

Yet A24 was able to maintain interest in the convicted fraudster, teasing out the secrets that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ‘s documentary promised to disclose without ever revealing its surprises. Audiences intent on not having the whole thing spoiled snapped up tickets, with A24 reporting that there were more than 2,000 sellouts.

The film ‘s success is a testament to a clever marketing campaign that by revealing next to nothing, somehow made “You Can See Everything” even more of an event . It’s also a credit to Nathan Fielder, the film’s co-director, who has cultivated a strong following through shows like Comedy Central’s “Nathan for You” and HBO’s “The Rehearsal,” that push meta to the breaking point. His awkward energy seemed perfectly matched for whatever Holmes is serving up through those unblinking eyes. Fielder’s co-director, Lance Oppenheim, is also riding high, having recently directed another A24 hit , the Robert Pattinson drama “Primetime.” That look at “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen has grossed nearly $45 million on a $14.5 million budget. “You Can See Everything” carries a $7 million budget, setting itself up for a very, very profitable run.

Last year at this time, A24 was in rough shape . It had raised $75 million in 2024 from Thrive Capital which valued the company at a massive $3.5 billion. Then it used that money to invest in some real duds, including “The Smashing Machine,” which cost $50 million and was supposed to score Dwayne Johnson an Oscar until it sunk like a rock at the box office , grossing a measly $21.1 million. Other costly flops included Ari Aster “Eddington,” which offered a return to the COVID era that audiences roundly rejected.

But since “Marty Supreme” opened in December of 2025, A24 has been on an epic hot streak. The drama about a ping-pong player became A24’s highest-grossing release ever, earning $192.4 million on a $70 million budget. But that record didn’t last long. “Backrooms” premiered in the summer, grossing more than $400 million on a $10 million budget. There have still been flops (justice for “Mother Mary”), but A24 hits like “Tony” and “The Drama” have outnumbered its misses. With major studios like Warner Bros. and Fox getting sold off or disappearing, A24 and its $3.5 billion valuation stand out like a beacon of hope to auteurs like Fielder and Oppenheim, promising them both artistic freedom and a chance to reach a wider audience than they otherwise might have dreamed of attracting.

Of course, it helps to have a killer marketing hook. In Holmes, an erstwhile entrepreneur who hoodwinked Beltway power brokers and captains of industry before lighting billions of dollars on fire, “You Can See Everything” demonstrates once again that nothing is as fascinating as a fall from grace.

article_text:
Charli xcx and Martin Scorsese ‘s collaboration is extending beyond the cover for her new album “Music, Fashion, Film.”

Sources tell Variety that the pop star has a cameo in the Oscar-winning director’s upcoming movie “What Happens at Night” alongside Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence . Described as a Gothic psychological drama, the Apple and StudioCanal production follows an American married couple who travel to a small European town to adopt a baby — but as they struggle to claim their child, the less they seem to know about themselves.

Related Stories

‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories

'You Can See Everything': That Shocking, Meta Twist With [SPOILER] Explained in Elizabeth Holmes Doc

Charli’s part in the film is being kept under wraps. She joins a cast that also includes Mads Mikkelsen, Patricia Clarkson and Jared Harris.

Representatives for Charli, Apple and StudioCanal did not immediately respond to Variety ‘s request for comment.

The “Brat” singer has been making a name for herself in the film world as of late, appearing in seven movies over the past two years. That includes “The Moment,” a mockumentary directed by her frequent collaborator Aidan Zamiri which cheekily satirized the commercial success she achieved with “Brat.” Cinema even inspired her latest album, “Music, Fashion, Film,” which pictures John Cale, Marc Jacobs and Scorsese on the cover to symbolize each art form. Charli is currently wrapping up her tour for the record in the U.S., with the final show of the leg in Las Vegas on Friday before she heads to Europe in February.

“What Happens at Night” marks Scorsese’s follow-up to 2023’s “Killers of the Flower Moon,” which also starred DiCaprio and was nominated for 10 Oscars, including best picture. A release date has not yet been set.

article_text:
F or a Halloween treat, here is a lavishly restored print of the 1958 Hammer Dracula, a fierce melodrama directed by Terence Fisher with Christopher Lee tremendously charismatic as the unspeakable Count, and Peter Cushing playing his enemy, Professor Van Helsing. It’s madly over-the-top, with Dracula’s lovely brides resplendent in their naughty nighties and negligées, and there is much hammy “reaction” acting – one character reacts to the contents of Dracula’s coffin as if he has been jabbed in the buttocks with an electric cattle-prod. But it’s often entertainingly creepy in a twilit world of its own.

Scriptwriter Jimmy Sangster pacily adapted Bram Stoker’s novel, speeding matters up by placing Professor Van Helsing’s base not in Yorkshire but in Germany, a country which here appears to have a very, very slackly policed border with the sovereign state of Transylvania. Character actor Miles Malleson has a strange cameo as an undertaker who has temporary charge of Dracula’s casket. (For my money, incidentally, the best Dracula adaptation is the 1977 BBC TV version with Louis Jourdan in the title role.)

Interestingly, Sangster’s script compares vampirism to drug addiction, explicitly bringing forward its metaphorical properties. For me it called to mind, yet again, Abel Ferrara’s superb horror-comic movie about vampires, The Addiction. This Hammer classic will be good for a laugh, and some shivers.

article_text:
Source: Dick Thomas Johnson, Wiki Commons CC BY 2.0

Yamazaki Takashi (cropped)

Takashi Yamazaki, the Japanese Oscar-winning director of Godzilla Minus One and the upcoming Godzilla Minus Zero , will make his English-language debut on Grandgear for Sony Pictures. J.J. Abrams’ Robot is producing.

Sam Nivola and Nico Parker have joined the production, and Paul Giamatti, who stars in A24’s awards hopeful The Debut , is understood to be in talks to join the cast. Yamazaki wrote the original screenplay however plot details remain under the proverbial wraps. Glen Zipper is producing alongside Abrams.

Yamazaki became the first director since Stanley Kubrick to win a visual effects Oscar with Godzilla Minus One in 2024. That film grossed $113m worldwide and Yamazaki’s follow-up, Godzilla Minus Zero , is scheduled to open in the US on November 6 through GKids.

Nivola earned an Actor Award nomination for The White Lotus and has starred in White Noise and Maestro . He stars in Hulu’s mystery series Phony that just premiered in the US.

UK actress Nico won the 2024 Sundance US Dramatic special jury award for breakthrough performance award for Searchlight’s Suncoast , and was nominated for a 2024 supporting actress Bafta for HBO series The Last Of Us . She also played the female lead in DreamWorks Animation’s live-action How To Train Your Dragon .

article_text:
In New York real estate , a good amenity can add serious dollars to the asking price: a private gym is nice, a rooftop pool even better. An original Keith Haring mural? That’ll tick the price up to $25 million.

A seven-bedroom loft containing a work the artist painted in 1979 has hit the market for $25 million, according to the New York Times . The catch? The mural is painted directly onto the building’s walls, ceiling, and structural supports, so the art literally comes with the listing (or vice versa). Related Articles Art Collector Beth Rudin DeWoody Lists Upper East Side Co-Op for $12 M. Jackson Pollock's Former West Village Loft Hits the Market for $1.99 M.

The 8,000-square-foot triplex occupies part of the American Thread Building at 260 West Broadway, a Renaissance Revival building completed in 1896. In addition to Haring’s black-and-white artwork, it has 28-foot ceilings, nine bathrooms, a screening room, a gym, and a sauna.

Haring painted the work in 1979, shortly after arriving in New York to study at the School of Visual Arts, which, at the time, used part of the building as a student exhibition space. Executed in a mixture of shoe polish and alcohol, the mural features the swirling, graphic forms and figures that would soon become hallmarks of his work.

The mural could easily have disappeared. After the school vacated the premises, the space was converted into a restaurant, and the mural was concealed behind wallboard. It remained hidden for decades before being uncovered in 2007 during renovations by previous owners.

As Tribeca Citizen reported, the discovery was first reported by New York magazine in 2008 . Architect Todd Ernst, who helped uncover the mural, compared the experience to discovering an Egyptian tomb. Remarkably, the water-soluble artwork had survived despite its proximity to a sprinkler pipe.

The apartment’s current owner, Adam Zoia, an executive in the recruiting industry, bought the apartment in 2021 and later undertook a two-year renovation. He told the Times that he recognized the unsigned mural immediately as a Haring. (The Keith Haring Foundation later authenticated the work, according to Zoia.)

During the renovation, Zoia installed a bar in front of the mural, partly to protect it from accidental damage. The artwork extends across an iron column, a beam, the ceiling, and the surrounding walls.

That presents an unusual problem for anyone hoping to put a price on it.

New York dealer Jenn Singer told the Times that the mural’s site-specific nature makes it nearly impossible to value separately from the property. Unlike a painting that can be removed, sold, and installed elsewhere, this Haring is effectively inseparable from the apartment. Zoia was less cautious about its potential value. Were it possible to remove the work, he said, it might be worth more than the apartment itself.

For now, the mural and the loft are being offered together through Ian Slater, Michael Koeneke, and Eduardo Martinez of Trove Partners at Compass.

article_text:
Los Angeles–area cultural institution the Huntington , which encompasses an art museum, library, and botanical garden, has announced this year’s gifts to its art collection funded by the Huntington’s Art Collectors’ Council. Each year, the council chooses works to acquire based on recommendations from the museum’s curators.

The five Art Collectors’ Council acquisitions span the 16th to the 21st centuries and encompass a range of media. The gifts build on the museum’s existing holdings while creating connections with its library and garden.

The earliest of these gifts is a 16th-century majolica plate made in Deruta, Italy, a leading center of majolica ceramics since the Renaissance. One of only 10 known Deruta dishes bearing verses by the Italian poet Francesco Petrarch, it complements the library’s rare editions of the poet’s works.

Also included in the group is a hanging scroll painted by the Chinese painter Zhang Chenglong at the turn of the 17th century. This nearly 10-foot-long work depicts Mount Tai, one of China’s Five Sacred Mountains, and leads the viewer’s eye along the pilgrimage routes to the mountain’s summit. Traditional landscape paintings such as this one inspired the Huntington’s own Chinese Garden, and the scroll will be the centerpiece of planned exhibition of Chinese garden paintings in 2029.

Created around 1620, a still life by Jan Breughel the Elder—son of Flemish Renaissance painter Peter Breughel the Elder—is the first European floral still life to enter the Huntington’s collection. Featuring a circlet of flowers along with a collection of imported luxuries such as a string of pearls and a Japanese lacquer box, it has a clear connection to the institution’s famed botanical garden.

Also new to the collection is a 1933 copper and gilt sculpture by California modernist artist Sargent Claude Johnson. Drawing on West African traditional masks, it is one of Johnson’s many works celebrating Black American life and beauty. It will join two pieces by Johnson already in the Huntington’s collection, as well as other works of the Harlem Renaissance by Charles White, Romare Bearden, and others. Johnson was the subject of an exhibition at the Huntington in 2024.

The fifth work, Raqib Shaw ’s Space Between Dreams – The Pragmatic Pessimist (2022–23), depicts the Kashmiri British artist in a vast frozen landscape, burning books for warmth. Drawing in part on Mughal miniature painting, work was also inspired by the Huntington’s collection of 18th-century Beauvais tapestries. The gift reunites it with its companion work, Space Between Dreams –The Perseverant Prophet , acquired by the Huntington in 2025.

In addition to works acquired through the Art Collectors’ Council, the Huntington has received several important gifts in 2026, among them a version of Robert Indiana ’s iconic LOVE sculpture, a group of watercolors by American modernists such as Joseph Stella and John Marin, and a pair of photograms by Abstract Expressionist artist Theodore Roszak.

article_text:
When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “ Clean Hands ” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers ( Zach Braff ) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke ( Esther McGregor ) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.

Related Stories

Anna Marsh on How Canal+ Group's M&A Activity Helps 'Challenge the Status Quo' and Why 'There's Just No Room for Error' in Fast-Moving Business

Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.

Popular on Variety

Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.

Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?

By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition.

As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.

Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.

Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.

McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.

To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.

title_original: The Questionnaire : Joachim Romain by Carole Schmitz
editorial_title_zh: 访谈录：Carole Schmitz 专访约阿希姆·罗曼（Joachim Romain）
editorial_excerpt_zh: 约阿希姆·罗曼（JOACHIM ROMAIN）——关注他人不再看到的事物 约阿希姆·罗曼专门在影像通常不再引起我们兴趣的地方审视它们。撕裂的…… 本文《访谈录：Carole Schmitz 专访约阿希姆·罗曼（Joachim Romain）》最初发布于 The Eye of Photography 摄影杂志。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "约阿希姆·罗曼（JOACHIM ROMAIN）——关注他人不再看到的事物", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "约阿希姆·罗曼专门在影像通常不再引起我们兴趣的地方审视它们。撕裂的海报、残缺的字母、匿名的面孔、褪色的城市标牌、视觉残渣：他的领域不在于宏大壮观的图像，而在于图像消逝后残存的事物。自其街头摄影生涯早期以来，他便一直在城市环境中提取那些日常目光已经习惯忽视的碎片，剥夺它们的废弃物身份，赋予其另一种存在。对罗曼而言，摄影本身即是位移。这种姿态贯穿于一种实践的核心，这种实践从未完全认同摄影、城市艺术、拼贴与装置之间的边界。他并不将这些媒介视为独立的领地，而是视作同一种目光的不同状态。摄影负责捕捉，挪用负责孤立，拼贴负责重组，而装置则再次带来位移。因此，比起图像本身，他更感兴趣的是当其上下文改变、当其失去原有功能并获得新的视觉张力时，它会变成什么样。一张撕裂的广告海报已不再仅仅是一张海报；一个残缺的字母在成为物质后已不再仅仅是一个标牌；从影像中撕下的面孔可以瞬间变成一个时代的肖像。这里正在运作一种当代考古学。但这是一门没有乡愁的考古学。罗曼并不寻求保存城市的痕迹；他让这些痕迹处于张力之中。他关注的是图像出现、消失、重叠并最终生成其自身记忆的方式。他的作品揭示了一座不断生产和消解自身表象的城市。通过它，他还质疑了我们与图像的关系：它们的无所不在、流通速度、过剩与陈旧，以及尽管它们大量繁殖却依然变得不可见的奇异能力。他的目光自然属于城市艺术的历史，雅克·维勒格莱（Jacques Villeglé）正是其中的标志性人物之一。然而对罗曼而言，这种传承绝不仅仅是简单的引用。维勒格莱将墙面变成了一个启示的空间，收集公共海报的匿名撕裂痕迹作为集体记忆的符号，而罗曼则在一个充斥着图像的景观中创作，这里的碎片不再仅仅来自街头。它还来自数字领域、商业、广告、屏幕以及一种全新的视觉经济——在这里，一切几乎都在瞬间被生产、消费和替换。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他在巴黎卡纳瓦莱博物馆（Musée Carnavalet）举办的雅克·维勒格莱回顾展中的参展，在这种语境下具有了特殊的共鸣。这使他的作品融入了一段不断自我重塑的历史：那些不一定凭空创造图像、而是懂得辨认一张已经存在于另一张之下的图像并赋予其第二生命的艺术家们。对罗曼而言，这种揭示的行为既通过摄影运作，也通过物质、手势和构图运作。正是这种位移的逻辑在罗曼加莱画廊（Galerie Laurent Rigail）的展览《碎片解构》（Défragmentation）中显现出来。与雅克·维勒格莱、昆汀·DMR（Quentin DMR）以及为此次展览聚首的其他艺术家一起，罗曼共同推动了对作为艺术材料的“碎片”的思考：城市的碎片、记忆的碎片、海报、照片或标志的碎片。然而，展览的标题几乎可以用来描述他自己的方法。解构并不单纯是将图像砸成碎片。它是为了改变这些碎片之间的关系，从而让其他东西显现出来。这个理念贯穿于他的整个创作。即使在拍照时，罗曼也并非单纯地记录。他进行挑选。他进行取景。他进行排除。通过决定去看什么的抉择，他已经在改变现实。“取景某一部分往往会让你忘记其余部分，”他在这次问答中说道。这句话可以作为理解他整个创作实践的关键。因为这正是他的艺术开始的地方：意识到观看永远是一种选择的行为，而一个碎片有时比一张完整的图像表达得更多。因此，他对摄影的关系与其说是纪实性的，不如说是批判性的。重要的不仅是图像展示了什么，还有它将什么留在了画框之外、它隐藏了什么，以及它突然让我们看到了什么。因此他反复关注细节、偶然性，以及那些“对其他人而言并不存在”的事物。罗曼在事物的表面寻找裂缝。他在那里寻找故事、张力，有时仅仅是一种情感。他的视觉实践延续了这种探究，却没有给出最终定论。他将视觉废弃物转化为材料，却拒绝剥离其混乱的本质。他没有清理碎片；他让碎片保留其流转的痕迹。或许，这正是他目光的独特性所在。在一个图像变得触手可得、可修饰、可复制的世界里，罗曼依然在寻找那些曾活过的图像，寻找那些仍然承载着自身消逝痕迹的图像。", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "JOACHIM ROMAIN — LOOKING AT WHAT OTHERS NO LONGER SEE"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Joachim Romain looks at images precisely where they generally cease to interest us. Torn posters, amputated letters, anonymous faces, faded urban signs, visual debris: His domain is not that of the spectacular image, but that of what remains after it. Since his early days in street photography, he has extracted fragments from the urban environment that the ordinary gaze has learned to overlook, removing them from their status as waste and giving them another existence. For Romain, to photograph is already to displace. This gesture lies at the heart of a practice that has never fully accepted the boundaries between photography, urban art, collage, and installation. He does not regard these mediums as separate territories, but as different states of the same gaze. Photography captures, appropriation isolates, collage recomposes, and installation displaces once again. What interests him, then, is less the image itself than what it becomes when its context changes when it loses its original function and acquires a new visual charge. An advertising poster is no longer simply a poster once it has been torn; a fragment of a letter is no longer merely a sign once it becomes material; a face torn from an image can suddenly become the portrait of an era. There is a form of contemporary archaeology at work here. But it is an archaeology without nostalgia. Romain does not seek to preserve the traces of the city; he puts them into tension. He is interested in the way images appear, disappear, overlap, and ultimately generate a memory of their own. His work reveals a city that is constantly producing and destroying its own representations. Through it, he also questions our relationship to images: their omnipresence, their speed of circulation, their obsolescence, and their strange ability, despite their proliferation, to become invisible. His gaze naturally belongs to a history of urban art in which Jacques Villeglé stands as one of its defining figures. Yet with Romain, the lineage is never simply a matter of quotation. Where Villeglé turned the wall into a space of revelation, collecting the anonymous tears of public posters as signs of a collective memory, Romain works within a landscape saturated with images, where the fragment no longer comes from the street alone. It also comes from the digital realm, commerce, advertising, screens, and a new visual economy in which everything is produced, consumed, and replaced almost instantaneously."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His participation in the exhibition devoted to Jacques Villeglé at the Musée Carnavalet takes on a particular resonance in this context. It places his work within a history that continually reinvents itself: that of artists who do not necessarily create their images from nothing but know how to recognize an image that is already there, buried beneath another, and give it a second life. For Romain, this act of revelation operates as much through photography as through material, gesture, and composition. It is precisely this logic of displacement that emerges in Défragmentation at Galerie Laurent Rigail. Alongside Jacques Villeglé, Quentin DMR, and the other artists brought together for the exhibition, Romain contributes to a reflection on the fragment as artistic material: a fragment of the city, of memory, of a poster, a photograph, or a sign. Yet the exhibition’s title could almost describe his own method. To defragment is not simply to break an image into pieces. It is to alter the relationships between those pieces in order to make something else appear. This idea runs throughout his work. Even when he photographs, Romain does not simply record. He selects. He frames. He excludes. Through the choice of what he decides to look at, he is already transforming reality. “Framing one part often makes you forget the rest,” he says in this questionnaire. The phrase could serve as a key to his entire practice. Because this is precisely where his art begins: in the awareness that looking is always an act of selection and that a fragment can sometimes say more than a complete image. His relationship to photography is therefore less documentary than critical. What matters is not only what the image shows, but what it leaves outside the frame, what it conceals, and what it suddenly allows us to see. Hence his recurring attention to detail, accident, and to that which is “not there for everyone else.” Romain searches for cracks in the surface of things. He finds stories there, tensions, sometimes simply an emotion. His visual practice extends this investigation without resolving it. He transforms visual waste into material but refuses to strip it of its disorder. He does not clean up the fragment; he allows it to retain the traces of its passage. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his gaze lies. In a world where images have become instantly available, retouched, and reproducible, Romain continues to search for those that have lived for images that still bear the marks of their own disappearance."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To look at the world with Joachim Romain is therefore to accept slowing down before what we have learned to pass without seeing. article_text:
JOACHIM ROMAIN — LOOKING AT WHAT OTHERS NO LONGER SEE

Joachim Romain looks at images precisely where they generally cease to interest us. Torn posters, amputated letters, anonymous faces, faded urban signs, visual debris: His domain is not that of the spectacular image, but that of what remains after it. Since his early days in street photography, he has extracted fragments from the urban environment that the ordinary gaze has learned to overlook, removing them from their status as waste and giving them another existence. For Romain, to photograph is already to displace. This gesture lies at the heart of a practice that has never fully accepted the boundaries between photography, urban art, collage, and installation. He does not regard these mediums as separate territories, but as different states of the same gaze. Photography captures, appropriation isolates, collage recomposes, and installation displaces once again. What interests him, then, is less the image itself than what it becomes when its context changes when it loses its original function and acquires a new visual charge. An advertising poster is no longer simply a poster once it has been torn; a fragment of a letter is no longer merely a sign once it becomes material; a face torn from an image can suddenly become the portrait of an era. There is a form of contemporary archaeology at work here. But it is an archaeology without nostalgia. Romain does not seek to preserve the traces of the city; he puts them into tension. He is interested in the way images appear, disappear, overlap, and ultimately generate a memory of their own. His work reveals a city that is constantly producing and destroying its own representations. Through it, he also questions our relationship to images: their omnipresence, their speed of circulation, their obsolescence, and their strange ability, despite their proliferation, to become invisible. His gaze naturally belongs to a history of urban art in which Jacques Villeglé stands as one of its defining figures. Yet with Romain, the lineage is never simply a matter of quotation. Where Villeglé turned the wall into a space of revelation, collecting the anonymous tears of public posters as signs of a collective memory, Romain works within a landscape saturated with images, where the fragment no longer comes from the street alone. It also comes from the digital realm, commerce, advertising, screens, and a new visual economy in which everything is produced, consumed, and replaced almost instantaneously.

His participation in the exhibition devoted to Jacques Villeglé at the Musée Carnavalet takes on a particular resonance in this context. It places his work within a history that continually reinvents itself: that of artists who do not necessarily create their images from nothing but know how to recognize an image that is already there, buried beneath another, and give it a second life. For Romain, this act of revelation operates as much through photography as through material, gesture, and composition. It is precisely this logic of displacement that emerges in Défragmentation at Galerie Laurent Rigail. Alongside Jacques Villeglé, Quentin DMR, and the other artists brought together for the exhibition, Romain contributes to a reflection on the fragment as artistic material: a fragment of the city, of memory, of a poster, a photograph, or a sign. Yet the exhibition’s title could almost describe his own method. To defragment is not simply to break an image into pieces. It is to alter the relationships between those pieces in order to make something else appear. This idea runs throughout his work. Even when he photographs, Romain does not simply record. He selects. He frames. He excludes. Through the choice of what he decides to look at, he is already transforming reality. “Framing one part often makes you forget the rest,” he says in this questionnaire. The phrase could serve as a key to his entire practice. Because this is precisely where his art begins: in the awareness that looking is always an act of selection and that a fragment can sometimes say more than a complete image. His relationship to photography is therefore less documentary than critical. What matters is not only what the image shows, but what it leaves outside the frame, what it conceals, and what it suddenly allows us to see. Hence his recurring attention to detail, accident, and to that which is “not there for everyone else.” Romain searches for cracks in the surface of things. He finds stories there, tensions, sometimes simply an emotion. His visual practice extends this investigation without resolving it. He transforms visual waste into material but refuses to strip it of its disorder. He does not clean up the fragment; he allows it to retain the traces of its passage. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his gaze lies. In a world where images have become instantly available, retouched, and reproducible, Romain continues to search for those that have lived for images that still bear the marks of their own disappearance.

To look at the world with Joachim Romain is therefore to accept slowing down before what we have learned to pass without seeing. A worn letter. A half-erased face. A torn poster. A fragment of the city. Nothing, apparently. And yet, within that almost nothing, the possibility of an image.

Website : www.joachimromain.com Instagram : @joachimromain

Actu : Exhibitions : « Défragmentation » from oct 14th to nov. 14th 2026 Galerie Laurent Rigail 40, rue Volta 75003 Paris

Participation to the exhibition « Paris à l’arraché » dedicated to Jacques Villeglé at Musée Carnavalet.

What was your first photographic trigger? Joachim Romain: My father was a photographer. For my 15th birthday, he gave me a Nikon EM.

A photographic memory from your childhood? Joachim Romain: Me on the beach, photographed by my father.

The camera of your childhood? Joachim Romain: Polaroid, of course.

The one you use today? Joachim Romain: Canon 6D.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Joachim Romain: Brassaï.

The image you wish you had taken? Joachim Romain: The Woodstock album cover. I would have done two crazy things.

The one that moved you the most? Joachim Romain: Lee Friedlander.

And the one that made you angry? Joachim Romain: Marine mammals caught in fishing nets.

Which photograph changed the world? Joachim Romain: “Tank Man,” in Tiananmen Square.

And which photograph changed your world? Joachim Romain: A worn-out letter B and a face on a poster, photographed in Sarajevo in 2006. That image profoundly changed my photographic work and the subjects I research today.

What interests you most in an image? Joachim Romain: Its emotion.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object? Joachim Romain: The one that isn’t there for everyone else.

Elliott Erwitt once said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? Joachim Romain: To some extent, yes. But why choose?

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Joachim Romain: For me, technique comes after the subject and the framing. But it remains a very important part, depending on the effect you want to achieve with your subject.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? Joachim Romain: Absolutely not.

What can make silence visible in a photograph? Joachim Romain: A detail.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Joachim Romain: The moment is unique and that’s everything.

Can a photograph be more truthful than reality? Joachim Romain: That’s where staging comes into play.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? Joachim Romain: Clearly. Focusing on one part often makes you forget the rest.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? Joachim Romain: For me, a testimony above all.

What makes a good photograph? Joachim Romain: The emotion it gives you.

What quality is essential to being a good photographer? Joachim Romain: Going out to find your subject and waiting for the right moment.

How do you choose your projects? Joachim Romain: They are connected to my visual art practice, although originally it was the other way around: my street photography gradually gave birth to my visual art practice. Today, the two have become one body of work in which photography and visual art come together.

How would you describe your creative process? Joachim Romain: It depends on the work. With the photographic series Fast_Shop , for example, there is a whole research process beforehand, followed by a real exploration of movement and time.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? Joachim Romain: My project Made in Europe is about creating an exhibition that brings my street work, photography, and installation into dialogue.

The person you would like to photograph? Joachim Romain: my daughter, and I did it! But I’d happily do it again.

The person you would like to be photographed by? Joachim Romain: Mari Katayama or Zanele Muholi.

One essential photography book? Joachim Romain: Affichage_Libre 🙂 Otherwise, Chernobyl by Robert Polidori. And a book by Brassaï, Brassaï: Picasso and the Photographs , or Vivian Maier.

What is the last photograph you took? Joachim Romain: Portraits of artists in Turkey, in Izmir.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok — and why? Joachim Romain: Instagram. There hasn’t been anything fun on Facebook for a while. And I’m not on TikTok at all.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? Joachim Romain: The quality, the framing… A bit like when digital photography arrived and everyone thought they were a photographer.

One Instagram account everyone should follow? Joachim Romain: Your friends’. The rest isn’t important.

What is your view on AI? Joachim Romain: A bit like when the first Adobe Illustrator came along: it’s a development that is difficult to avoid, but one we need to learn to master. The most important thing, in my view, is to remain the creative force, rather than simply following or letting AI do the creating for us. But, in reality, I think we won’t be in control of much for very long.

Color or black and white? Joachim Romain: Both, but with a preference for black and white.

Natural or artificial light? Joachim Romain: Natural.

Which city strikes you as the most photogenic? Joachim Romain: Marseille.

The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering? Joachim Romain: Africa.

The place you never get tired of? Joachim Romain: My bathroom 🙂 Seriously, though, definitely the Arles festival.

The image that, for you, represents the state of the world today? Joachim Romain: The photomontage of British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking a selfie against a backdrop of burning oil.

What do you think is missing from the world today? Joachim Romain: A strong movement toward nature and living together. It’s frightening right now.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you go for a selfie with him? Joachim Romain: That’s too disconnected from reality for me, so…

Your favorite drug? Joachim Romain: My studio.

Your best way to switch off? Joachim Romain: I haven’t found one. I dream of it.

Your latest act of madness? Joachim Romain: A Get 27–Ricard cocktail in Arles 🙂 I still have a headache.

The body of work you are particularly proud of? Joachim Romain: My Urban work, which consists of transforming what everyone considers visual waste into an art installation.

The job you would never have wanted to do? Joachim Romain: I respect people so much that saying “I wouldn’t want to do your job” feels a bit harsh 🙂

Which question throws you off the most? Joachim Romain: Who is your favorite artist?

The last thing you did for the first time? Joachim Romain: Rowing on the Olympic rowing basin in Montreal, with my family. It was great.

Your biggest regret? Joachim Romain: Not having gone to art school.

If you could start all over again? Joachim Romain: Maybe I would have taken school more seriously. But then again, I wouldn’t have had the path I’ve had, and I don’t regret it.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table? Joachim Romain: Jim Morrison, Nina Kraviz, Jacques Villeglé, Anselm Kiefer. Music and art: everything I love.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? Joachim Romain: If they remember me at all, that’s already something 🙂

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? Joachim Romain: Generous.

One last word? Joachim Romain: Together.

Source: A24

‘You Can See Everything’

A24’s You Can See Everything expanded in its second session at the North American box office and is nearing $50m, while DC Studios’ Clayface opened top of the charts on a confirmed $24m for the combined Paramount-Warner Bros.

This was a respectable launch in 3,458 sites for the R-rated body horror Clayface , which earned an A- Cinemascore and is on solid footing given the reported $44m production cost. Tom Rhys Harries stars in the Batman spin-off about an up-and-coming film star who embarks on a revenge spree after a medical procedure goes wrong. James Watkins directed.

Meanwhile the enduring fascination with You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Oscar-tipped meta investigation into truth and fiction featuring Elizabeth Holmes and others, showed no signs of letting up. It expanded into 2,655 sites as box office increased by 25% and the film added $19.5m for a $45.1m running total.

The R-rated three-hour feature already ranks as one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. It earned $6.1m on Friday, $6.9m on Saturday, and $6.4m on Sunday. A24 executives will feel vindicated after last weekend’s platform release led to nationwide sell-outs and increased demand from audiences.

Fathom Entertainment opened Laika’s acclaimed Wildwood at number three and reported $12.3m from 2,779 sites. FilmNation handles international sales. Paramount’s Street Fighter fell 72% in its second weekend to rank fourth on $8.6m from 3,575 for $46.9m.

Black Bear opened its Sundance pick-up Wicker starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard in fifth place on $5.8m. Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson directed the romantic tale set in a village centuries ago where an ostracised fisherwoman asks a basketweaver to make her a husband, with surprising results. Wicker drew a 79% female, 45% white and 42% 25-43 demographic.

In its second weekend Netflix expanded La Bola Negra into nine cinemas and the Spanish Oscar submission and awards season heavyweight earned $245,000 for an early $650,000 running total. The contender will remain in its exclusive theatrical run until it drops on Netflix on December 2.

Since boarding the documentary NAZA as US distributor last week, Neon reported that the film has crossed $1m after four weekends in release. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s interview-based account of Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers discussing the killing of Palestinians added a confirmed $75,000 from 73 screens and stands at $1.1m. Warner Bros Clockwork reported that Ken Russell’s The Devils stands at a confirmed $3.1m after adding $415,000 from 315 locations in the second session.

Overall box office for the weekend added $94.9m per Rentrak, marking a 21.8% climb against the comparable session in 2025. Year-to-date earnings have reached $8.4bn and track 20.2% ahead of 2025 by the same stage.

article_text:
Films and events

Thrill

The Match

Few sporting contests loom as large in the public imagination as the dramatic 1986 World Cup Quarter Final between England and Argentina, as this documentary details.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriters Juan Cabral, Santiago Franco

With Gary Lineker, Jorge Valdano

Argentina-Spain 2026. 91min

Courtesy of Walt Disney Studios

Languages English, Spanish With English subtitles

Introduction

England players, including Gary Lineker and John Barnes, assemble with their Argentine counterparts to relive the famed ‘hand of god’ match, which is artfully juxtaposed against the geopolitical conflict that proceeded it. Based on Andrés Burgo’s book, Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco have crafted one of the most thrilling documentaries of the year, infusing history and politics with the excitement and import of this legendary match.

Kristy Matheson

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Heysel 85

This is a gripping and sobering dramatic reconstruction of the tragedy that unfolded during the 1985 European Cup final between Liverpool and Juventus at the Brussels stadium.

Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing

Erik Shirai’s beautifully shot and fascinating film grants rare access inside the disciplined inner domain of Japan’s sumo wrestling world.

Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff

This awe-inspiring documentary is a detailed and thought-provoking portrait of the astronomer and astrophysicist behind Cosmos and Contact.

つりこまち

劇場公開日： 2026年11月27日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

スクウェア・エニックス「ヤングガンガン」で連載された山崎夏軌のガールズフィッシング漫画「つりこまち」を実写映画化し、釣りに熱中する女子高校生たちの友情と成長を描いた青春ドラマ。 館山真理萌（マリモ）は9歳にして天才釣り少女と呼ばれていたが、水難事故で母親を亡くしたことをきっかけに、釣りに夢を求めることができなくなってしまう。高校生になった彼女は釣具店を営む祖母と2人暮らしで、祖母はそんなマリモを心配しながらも温かく見守っていた。ある日、天才釣り少女のマリモに憧れる高校生・テトラがアメリカからやってくる。「2年後のオリンピックで世界一の釣り師になる」という情熱的なテトラとの出会いを通して釣りへの熱い想いを取り戻したマリモは、親友・乃莉に協力してもらいながら、釣りでオリンピック金メダルを目指すことになる。 真理萌役で仲村悠菜（私立恵比寿中学）が映画初主演を果たし、真理萌の親友・乃莉役で吉本此那（僕が見たかった青空）、真理萌を取り巻くライバル役で暁月ななみ（KAGURAMUSOU）、鹿目凛、石浜芽衣（虹のコンキスタドール）が共演。

editorial_title_zh: 《Larger Than Life》展评——超级无敌掌门狗、小羊肖恩和伙伴们为这部爆笑的阿德曼起源故事大声说“茄子”
editorial_excerpt_zh: Lightroom，伦敦 从肖恩的谷仓到格罗特的纸箱，这些咧着大嘴、淘气的角色的沉浸式幕后呈现欢乐、巨大——而且有点难以捉摸 沉浸化大潮无孔不入。他们把古斯塔夫·克里姆特和文森特…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "沉浸化的大潮无孔不入。他们把古斯塔夫·克里姆特（Gustav Klimt）和文森特·梵高（Vincent Van Gogh）变成了巨大的投影数字环境；他们把登月、恐龙和大卫·鲍伊（David Bowie）的故事做成了从地面到天花板的电子视觉盛宴；现在，他们又盯上了阿德曼（Aardman）。为了超级无敌掌门狗和笑笑羊（Shaun the Sheep）这两个我们的国民级珍宝。难道就没有什么是神圣不可侵犯的吗？", "links": [{"text": "Aardman", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/aardman"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这场在 Lightroom 举办的最新沉浸式光影体验，是对阿德曼动画（Aardman Animations）的一次盛大、惊艳的礼赞，这家公司正是世界上最受欢迎的粘土动画电影和剧集背后的缔造者。它在纪录片叙事、幕后解密以及对所有你所熟悉、咧着大嘴且淘气的北方角色的炫目沉浸式呈现之间自由切换。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们得以聆听彼得·洛德（Peter Lord）和大卫·斯普罗克斯顿（David Sproxton）如何在萨里的郊区相遇并开始摆弄粘土，随后与尼克·帕克（Nick Park）联手，开启了一系列将他们从沃金（Woking）带向星辰大海的旅程。我们了解到他们最初是如何用一个粘土球捏出 Morph 的，动画师们如何在面对镜头时滑稽地亲自演遍所有场景再转到木偶身上，他们又是如何让嘴巴做出念出“cheese”这个词时的“eeee”音，这一切还穿插着笑笑羊在谷仓里举办的才艺秀以及他们最伟大电影成就的片段。", "links": [{"text": "Peter Lord and David Sproxton", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2026/aug/23/aardman-animations-founders-peter-lord-david-sproxton-interview-oscars-wallace-gromit-chicken-run"}, {"text": "Nick Park", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2009/nov/02/nick-park-film-maker"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9aa9d6c1388bc126a02be32a5fb967af7ca1b3b1/1537_36_7151_5719/master/7151.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Larger than Life - 全新阿德曼动画沉浸式展", "caption": "“电影什么时候开始？”……一名儿童在 Lightroom 的屏幕前伸出手。摄影：Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KX", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它为阿德曼为何如此重要、为何深受如此多人的喜爱给出了一个相当有说服力的论点。刚开场不久，它就剪入了1989年《超级无敌掌门狗：月球野餐记》（A Grand Day Out）中的一个片段，这是第一部超级无敌掌门狗电影。在这个巨大的尺度下，你可以看到粘土中的每一个疙瘩和凸起、每一个指纹和污迹。它看起来是那么真实、那么具有人性。导演露西·伊扎德（Lucy Izzard）在旁白中说：“我认为人们依然渴望不完美，”你会觉得没错，就是这样，这就是阿德曼重要的原因。在一个很多时候一切都显得无比非人的时代里，它包含着某种极其具人性的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种手工制作的、不完美的、充满家常气息的美学，与沉浸式电影的技术魔力之间是否存在着尴尬的摩擦？当然有。但更大的问题在于，这次体验并没有真正弄清楚它自己到底想成为什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它最终变成了一半纪录片、一半剪辑集，在这个过程中两边不讨好，而且也有点让人难以跟上。它甚至没有充分利用 Lightroom 的各项功能。它本可以更大胆、更有趣，本可以对沉浸式这种形式做更多的把玩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这项技术的良好运用之一是侧边屏幕，它能让你感觉自己身处各种不同的环境之中：笑笑羊的谷仓、格罗特监视费沙·麦格劳（Feathers McGraw）时的纸箱，或是演员们进行配音录制时的录音台后方。但这些还远远不够。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这里确实有一些有趣的内容。看到《动物庄园》（Creature Comforts）在起居室和花园里重现感觉很棒，看到所有的概念艺术和故事板活过来也很不错，看着彼得·加布里埃尔（Peter Gabriel）《Sledgehammer》那惊人的 MV 以如此巨大的规模呈现更是令人愉悦。它只是缺乏 Lightroom 最近推出的《史前星球：探索恐龙》（Prehistoric Planet: Discovering Dinosaurs）那种广受欢迎的沉浸式震撼感。", "links": [{"text": "Peter Gabriel’s Sledgehammer", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OJWJE0x7T4Q"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ad3fba0e45565aad7eb49aecdbf878efccd27927/0_0_8688_5792/master/8688.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "全新的阿德曼动画在 Lightroom 上投影呈现。", "caption": "“这算是一种纪录片。”摄影：Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KX", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一个饱经沧桑、疲惫不堪的当代艺术评论人，我或许并非其目标受众，所以我带上了一个名叫所罗门（Solomon）的人。他的资质是什么？好吧，他四岁，昨天刚去电影院看了最新的笑笑羊电影，所以你大可以称他为某种年轻的影迷。此外，他的父亲（也就是我）是个评论人，因此他大概在基因上就倾向于对此产生各种看法。", "links": [{"text": "the latest Shaun the Sheep article_text:
N othing is safe from the scourge of immersification. They’ve turned Gustav Klimt and Vincent Van Gogh into vast, projection-mapped digital environments; they’ve told the stories of the moon landings and the dinosaurs and David Bowie as floor-to-ceiling electronic spectacles; and now they’ve come for Aardman . For Wallace and Gromit and Shaun the Sheep, our national treasures. Is nothing sacred?

The latest immersive cinematic experience at Lightroom is a big, eye-popping celebration of Aardman Animations, the company behind the world’s favourite claymation films and TV shows. It moves between documentary storytelling, behind-the-scenes insight and dazzling immersive renderings of all your wide-grinned, cheeky northern favourites.

We get to hear about how Peter Lord and David Sproxton met in suburban Surrey and started messing around with clay, before joining forces with Nick Park and setting in motion a series of events that would take them from Woking to the stars. We get to hear about how they first made Morph out of a ball of clay, how the animators hilariously act out all the scenes to camera themselves before moving over to puppets, how they make the mouths form the “eeee” sound of the word cheese, all interspersed with Shaun the Sheep doing a barn-based talent show and clips from their biggest cinematic triumphs.

And it makes a pretty convincing argument for why Aardman is so important, so beloved by so many people. Early on, it cuts to a clip from 1989’s A Grand Day Out, the first Wallace & Gromit film. At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay, every finger print and smudge. It looks so real, so human. Director Lucy Izzard says in a voiceover: “I think people still crave imperfection,” and you think yes, that’s it, that’s why Aardman matters. It’s something incredibly human in an age when things feel so amazingly non-human so much of the time.

Does that hand-made, imperfect, homely aesthetic rub up awkwardly against the technological wizardry of immersive cinema? Sure does. But the bigger issue is that this experience doesn’t really know what it wants to be.

It ends up as half-documentary, half-clip show, becoming sort of neither in the process, and a bit hard to follow too. It doesn’t even take full advantage of Lightroom’s capabilities. It could be bolder, more fun, it could play with the immersive format a bit more.

One good use of the tech are the side screens, which make you feel like you are inside various environments: Shaun the Sheep’s barn, Gromit’s cardboard box as he spies on Feathers McGraw, behind the recording desk as actors do their vocal takes. But it’s not quite enough.

There’s some fun stuff here. It’s great seeing Creature Comforts recreated in living rooms and gardens, it’s nice to see all the concept art and storyboards come to life, it’s pretty joyful watching the amazing video for Peter Gabriel’s Sledgehammer at such an enormous scale. It just lacks the crowd-pleasing immersive thrills of Lightroom’s recent Prehistoric Planet: Discovering Dinosaurs.

As a jaded, tired contemporary art critic, I may not be the target audience, so I brought along someone called Solomon. What are his qualifications? Well, he’s four, and yesterday he went to the cinema to see the latest Shaun the Sheep movie , so you could say he’s something of a young cinephile. Also, his father (me) is a critic, so he is probably genetically predisposed to have opinions about this.

Halfway through, I ask what he thinks. He says: “When is the movie starting? This is just ads.” He’s right – the whole thing just feels like an advert for Aardman. “When is the movie starting?” he asks again, more impatient this time, almost pleading. “This is it,” I say. “It’s sort of a documentary.” He stares at me, uncomprehending, and then yawns. Ouch, he really is a critic.

It doesn’t really have enough for kids, and the storytelling isn’t strong enough for adults. It’s gimmick over narrative, as if they didn’t ask: “How can we make an amazing immersive experience?” but instead asked: “How can we tell our story in an immersive-ish way?” And those are two different propositions.

This show doesn’t tarnish Aardman’s stellar reputation, nor detract from all the amazing, quirky, quaint, funny work that they’ve done, but it doesn’t add a huge amount to it either. More of a rubber glove on the head than a crowning achievement.

article_text:
Shares of Skydance Corp., formed through the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, fell as much as 27% in trading Wednesday. The drop came as the Skydance, led by chairman and CEO David Ellison, distributed about 471 million warrants giving holders of Paramount Skydance’s PSKY Class B shares the option to purchase stock in the new company.

Skydance’s stock — which began trading Oct. 6 on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol “SKYD” — closed down 22.2%, to $7.06/share, as of the end of regular trading Wednesday.

Related Stories

Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC

'Amanda the Adventurer' Video Game Movie Adaptation in the Works From Blumhouse, MatPat and Epic Pictures

Each warrant issued to PSKY holders initially allows them to buy one share of Skydance for $12. (The warrants, trading on NYSE under “SKYD.WS,” had an Oct. 13 closing price of $2.20 apiece. PSKY stock was delisted from the Nasdaq on Oct. 5.) If all of those warrants were exercised, that would raise about $5.65 billion for the company, while it would also increase the share count and dilute ownership of current shareholders. It’s not known how many warrants have been exercised so far. Holders of the warrants have up to 10 years (until 2036) to exercise the warrants

In connection with Skydance’s distribution of stock warrants to PSKY holders, the NYSE announced after market close Tuesday that it would adjust the official closing price of Skydance’s Class B common stock downward by $0.19368 per share (from approximately $9.27 to approximately $9.07) based on the official closing price of the warrants at $2.20 each, a pro-rata calculation for the approximately 9% that 471 million shares of Class B common stock entitled to receive a warrant represents of shares outstanding.

According to Skydance, the pre-warrant market capitalization of the company was $46.6 billion (at a price of $9.27/share for Class B shares). The implied value with the warrants would have given Skydance a market cap of $45.6 billion at the $9.07/share price of the Class B stock. With the stock drop Wednesday, the market cap stood at around $35.6 billion.

The warrants issued to PSKY shareholders are intended to provide them the opportunity to purchase shares of Skydance’s Class B common stock “on similar terms” to those offered to the parties in the $47 billion equity syndicate backing the Warner Bros. Discovery deal, including David Ellison; his father, Larry Ellison; Gerry Cardinale, managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners; LionTree; and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Those equity investments in SKYD were priced at $12 per share.

While the movement of Skydance’s stock price Wednesday has more to do with the issuing of the stock warrants, Wall Street has not been bullish on the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. The company will have pro-forma annual revenue of nearly $70 billion — but it also will have to deal with almost $80 billion in net debt .

The distribution of the warrants “marks the final step in the WBD transaction closing process,” Wells Fargo analysts led by Steven Cahall said in a research note published Wednesday morning. They noted that “media mergers have a less than ideal history in terms delivering on pro-forma EBITDA expectations,” citing CBS and Viacom, Disney and 21st Century Fox and Discovery and WarnerMedia.

That said, the Wells Fargo analysts wrote, “We think SKYD will successfully deliver its ~$6bn in planned cost synergies. The main risk is whether the integration and disruption causes some leakage in core ops, and/or whether Media fundamentals change or are disrupted by tech. This history means investors may discount pro forma EBITDA to account for the leverage & risk.” The firm has an “underweight” rating on Skydance’s stock with a 12-month price target of $7.00/share.

The Paramount-WBD deal, valued at $111 billion including the assumption of WBD debt, brings together two major studios, TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV and TBS, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Last week, after the deal closed, Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz (former chief of Mattel) announced their senior executive leadership team for the new Skydance.

article_text:
金沢の国立工芸館で 10 月 9 日、「デザイン・クロニクル展 なにが生まれて、なにが変わった？」が開幕しました。モリスやミュシャ、ラリック、イームズなど、人気作家の名品がズラリと並ぶ展示室で、工芸とデザインの奥深い世界を体感できる展覧会です。

日本で唯一の美術館！

国立工芸館は、その名称から美術工芸品を扱うイメージがありますが、実はデザインに関する作品も多く所蔵しています。

本展を担当した国立工芸館・主任研究員の三木敬介さんによると、コレクションの約 23 パーセントがデザイン分野に関する作品で、日本で唯一、工芸とデザインを専門に扱う珍しい美術館だそうです。

工芸とは？ デザインとは？

では、何が工芸で、何がデザインなのでしょう？

「簡単には説明できませんが、大きな違いは、熟練職人や作家が一貫して手仕事で制作したものが工芸品で、考える人と実際に作る人が別になっているのがデザイン分野の作品です」（三木さん）

かつて、工芸品は工芸家が自ら作り上げていたのですが、 19 世紀の工業化によって「ものづくり」が変化。デザイナーが形や装飾を考案し、工場で大量生産するようになりました。

本展では、「デザイン」という考え方が生まれ、変化していく軌跡を、名品とともに辿ることができます。

時代を代表するデザイナーの作品が勢ぞろい

会場には、インテリアや食器など、身近な作品が並んでいます。しかも、各時代を代表するデザイナーが生み出した上質なものばかり。時空を超えた最高峰のセレクトショップと言っても良さそうな雰囲気です。

展示作品は、アーツ＆クラフツ運動からはじまり、デザイン史に合わせて時系列で紹介されています。立体だけでなく平面の作品もあるのがユニークで、ポスターデザインの先駆者、ミュシャの作品もありました。

アール・デコを代表する作家、ラリックの作品は、今の時代に見てもモダンです。作品名の「ラガマール」とは、古代メソポタミアの神の名前。壁画のような文様とモノトーンの色彩がステキですね。

いくつか家電も展示されています。 1940 年に制作されたハンディ・クリーナーは、この時代に流行した機関車の流線形デザインを取り入れているそうです。自宅にある掃除機のルーツもここにあるのかな、と想像すると楽しいです。

ドイツの総合デザイン学校、バウハウスで学んだ人たちの作品は、どれも使いやすそうに見えます。アール・ヌーヴォーやアール・デコのような装飾はなくシンプルですが、機能美を備えています。

名作椅子を体感！

椅子の展示も見どころのひとつ。各時代の椅子を見比べることができます。

ブロイヤーが考案したワシリーチェアは、椅子の歴史を変えた名作。当時、椅子といえば、木製の四本足が主流でしたが、ブロイヤーは自転車のフレームに着想を得て、スチールパイプを使った足にしました。

ディクソンの《鉄塔の椅子》は、世界最軽量を目指した椅子。鋼線を溶接して作られていますが、アート作品のような美しさです。

ちなみに、 1 階の「工芸とであう」のコーナーでは、ワシリーチェアをはじめ、いくつかの名作椅子に座ることができます。

展示を見終わったあとワシリーチェアに座ったのですが、椅子の常識を変えたデザインだと思うと、感慨深いものがありました。

この展覧会は、デザイン史を考えながら見るといろいろな発見が得られますし、また、かわいい食器やおしゃれな日用品も多いので、眺めているだけでも楽しいです。

秋の金沢は、観光しやすいベストシーズンです。ぜひ、展覧会にあわせて訪れてみてください。（取材・文：ライター・田代わこ）

デザイン・クロニクル展 なにが生まれて、なにが変わった？

会場：国立工芸館（石川県金沢市出羽町3-2）

会期： 2026 年 10 月 9 日 ( 金 ) 〜 2027 年 1 月 11 日 ( 月・祝） ※ 会期中一部展示替えあり ［前期： 2026 年 10 月 9 日 ( 金 ) 〜 11 月 23 日 ( 月･祝 ) 後期： 2026 年 11 月 25 日 ( 水 ) 〜 2027 年 1 月 11 日 ( 月･祝 ) ］

article_text:
⁠Jurandir Filho ⁠, ⁠ Rogério Montanare ⁠, ⁠ Thiago Siqueira ⁠ e ⁠ Fernanda Bermoltz ⁠ batem um papo nostálgico sobre o ano de 1996 nos cinemas!! Esse podcast é mais uma edição da série ⁠ We Have to Go Back ⁠ , onde voltamos no tempo e revisitamos os grandes filmes de um ano específico. Além disso, é um programa nostálgico, pois relembramos os acontecimentos desse ano, as músicas, as evoluções tecnológicas, os jogos de videogames, as curiosidades, os costumes e muito mais!!

Falamos sobre “Um Drink no Inferno”, “Twister”, “O Corcunda de Notre Dame”, “Missão-Impossível”, “Matilda”, “Independence Day”, “Pânico”, “A Rocha”, “Jerry Maguire”, “101 Dálmatas”, “Space Jam”, “Trainspotting”, “Romeu + Julieta” e muito mais.

title_original: Jafar Panahi faces five-year prison sentence in Iran
editorial_title_zh: 贾法尔·帕纳西在伊朗面临五年有期徒刑
editorial_excerpt_zh: 曾获金棕榈奖、获奥斯卡提名的电影《It Was Just An Accident》的导演目前身在伊朗。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://d1nslcd7m2225b.cloudfront.net/Pictures/480xAny/9/0/2/1490902_img_0606_645474_crop.jpg", "alt": "贾法尔·帕纳西", "caption": "", "credit": "Screen Daily", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "来源：Screen 档案库", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贾法尔·帕纳西", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据其律师透露，伊朗电影人贾法尔·帕纳西已被德黑兰一家法院缺席判处五年零一个月监禁、没收全部资产并禁止出境两年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "根据德黑兰革命法院第26分庭下达的裁决，这位曾凭《It Was Just An Accident》斩获金棕榈奖并获奥斯卡提名的导演还被禁止在两年内从事社交媒体活动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "帕纳西的律师穆斯塔法·尼利（Mostafa Nili）表示，帕纳西的银行账户于上周被冻结，这促使他们向负责文化和媒体事务的检察官办公室进行查询，从而发现在帕纳西未收到听证会通知的情况下，法院已经下达了新的判决。导致最新定罪的具体指控尚未向公众澄清。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据尼利称，法庭文件声称帕纳西当时在国外且无法联系，尽管他已于3月30日返回伊朗，并于8月因另一起案件出席了调查法庭。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其律师表示，目前身在伊朗的帕纳西正面临三起进行中的法律诉讼。在此次最新裁决之前，他于2025年12月因“进行反对体制的宣传活动”被判罪名成立，获刑一年并禁止出境两年，上诉后维持原判。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这位电影人此前曾在2010年被判处六年监禁，并被禁止从事电影制作、编剧和国际旅行20年。他于2022年7月被捕以执行该刑期，在德黑兰的埃文监狱服刑七个月后，于2023年2月获释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "帕纳西与伊朗当局的屡次冲突，长期以来与他在国际上享有盛誉的电影人地位形成鲜明对比。尽管屡遭判刑和工作限制，他仍持续拍片并斩获各大电影节大奖，从1995年凭《白气球》获得戛纳电影节金 caméra d’Or（金摄影机奖）、2000年凭《生命的圆圈》获得威尼斯电影节金狮奖，到2015年凭《出租车》获得柏林电影节金熊奖。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他的最新长片《It Was Just An Accident》于2025年荣获戛纳电影节金棕榈奖，并在2026年奥斯卡金像奖上获得最佳国际影片和最佳原创剧本两项提名。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "帕纳西还出演了巴西导演小克莱伯·门东萨执导的短片《South Of Tehran》，该片探讨了他早年在德黑兰对电影的热爱，并于2025年纽约电影节上首映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "2026年电影节与市场日历：最新日期", "links": [{"text": "2026 film festivals and markets calendar: latest dates", "url": "https://www.screendaily.com/news/2026-film-festivals-and-markets-calendar-latest-dates/5211872.article"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://d1nslcd7m2225b.cloudfront.net/Pictures/480xAny/9/0/2/1490902_img_0606_645474_crop.jpg", "alt": "Jafar Panahi", "caption": "", "credit": "Screen Daily"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Source: Screen File"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jafar Panahi"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi has been sentenced in absentia to five years and one month in prison, the confiscation of all his assets and a two-year travel ban by a Tehran court, according to his lawyer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The director of Palme d’Or-winning, Oscar-nominated film It Was Just An Accident has also been banned from engaging in social media activities for two years under the ruling issued by Branch 26 of Tehran’s Revolutionary Court."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Panahi’s lawyer Mostafa Nili said the filmmaker’s bank accounts were frozen last week, prompting enquiries with the prosecutor’s office responsible for culture and media, where they discovered that a new sentence had been handed down without Panahi having been notified of the hearing. Source: Screen File

Jafar Panahi

Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi has been sentenced in absentia to five years and one month in prison, the confiscation of all his assets and a two-year travel ban by a Tehran court, according to his lawyer.

The director of Palme d’Or-winning, Oscar-nominated film It Was Just An Accident has also been banned from engaging in social media activities for two years under the ruling issued by Branch 26 of Tehran’s Revolutionary Court.

Panahi’s lawyer Mostafa Nili said the filmmaker’s bank accounts were frozen last week, prompting enquiries with the prosecutor’s office responsible for culture and media, where they discovered that a new sentence had been handed down without Panahi having been notified of the hearing. The charges underlying the latest conviction have not been publicly clarified.

According to Nili, court documents claimed Panahi was abroad and unreachable, despite his return to Iran on March 30 and an appearance before an investigative court in August in connection with a separate case.

Panahi, who is currently in Iran, faces three ongoing legal proceedings, according to his lawyer. The latest ruling follows a December 2025 conviction for “propaganda activities against the regime”, which carried a one-year prison sentence and two-year travel ban and was upheld on appeal.

The filmmaker was previously sentenced in 2010 to six years in prison and a 20-year ban on filmmaking, screenwriting and international travel. Arrested in July 2022 to serve that sentence, he spent seven months in Tehran’s Evin Prison before his release in February 2023.

Panahi’s repeated clashes with Iranian authorities have long contrasted with his standing as one of the country’s most internationally acclaimed filmmakers. Despite successive prison sentences and restrictions on his work, he has continued to make films and collect major festival honours, from the Caméra d’Or at Cannes for The White Balloon in 1995 to Venice’s Golden Lion for The Circle in 2000 and Berlin’s Golden Bear for Taxi in 2015.

His latest feature, It Was Just An Accident , won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2025 and received two nominations at the 2026 Academy Awards, for best international feature and best original screenplay.

Panahi also featured in South Of Tehran , a short film by Brazilian director Kleber Mendonça Filho exploring his early love of cinema in Tehran, which premiered at the 2025 New York Film Festival.
